name: Telegraph cryptic crossword, All New book 4 No 67

book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

clue.text: Things made earlier than absolutely necessary

definitions.text: Things made earlier than absolutely necessary

blocks.clueFragment: Things made earlier than absolutely necessary
blocks.note: surface reading: jobs done ahead of time, before anyone needed them
setter's reading: items built in advance, in a factory, ready to be put together on site later

explanation.surface: Someone frets about having done work sooner than it was ever needed.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'made earlier' as manufactured beforehand: prefabricated parts are made off site long before the building that uses them, and fabrications can also be lies made up in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: Prefabrications are building components manufactured ahead of assembly, so they are literally things made beforehand.

clue.text: Fact — posh peer composes a class of words

indicators.note: to compose is to put together into a new arrangement, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grand nobleman writes out a grammatical category for the record.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar sorts words into groups such as noun, verb and adjective; each group is called this.

clue.text: Giant comes up with a little knitted garment.

indicators.note: a little of something is only part of it, so the letters sit inside a longer word
in a down clue, coming up means reading from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: the letters run inside the word knitted

explanation.surface: A huge man appears holding a small woolly jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: An ettin is a two-headed giant of English folklore, also known from fantasy games.
explanation.definitionFit: Ettin is an old English word for a giant, surviving in folk tales and fantasy fiction.

clue.text: Gymnastic accountant accepts swindle at institute

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the other pieces go inside

blocks.note: acc. is an abbreviation for accountant or account
to rob is to cheat or steal from
taken as written
I is a standard abbreviation for institute

explanation.surface: An agile bookkeeper takes part in a fraud at some institution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gymnastic accountant' reads as one character, but the first word is the definition; the swindle, the 'at' and the institute join up before the accountant takes them in.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrobatic means agile in the manner of an acrobat, which is what gymnastic describes.

clue.text: Prevents taking holidays around the island

indicators.note: around means encircling here, so one word is wrapped about the other

blocks.note: rests are breaks from work
Is is an abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Something stops people going on holiday round an island.
explanation.definitionFit: To resist something is to withstand or hold it off, close to preventing it.

clue.text: Runs at full speed through the courses of life

blocks.note: first meaning: rushes headlong, as a runaway vehicle does
second meaning: people's working lives and progress over time

explanation.walkthrough: As a verb the word means to hurtle along; as a plural noun it means paths through working life.
explanation.definitionFit: To career is to rush wildly, and careers are the progressions people follow through their lives.

clue.text: Subject twitching about work

indicators.note: about means surrounding here, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a tic is a twitch
op. is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A theme concerning nervous jerks at the office.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is the theme or matter under discussion, the subject.

clue.text: Waste money getting lots of balls to hang

blocks.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls
pend is an old verb meaning to hang

explanation.surface: Someone squanders cash buying heaps of balls to hang up.
explanation.walkthrough: An over is cricket's unit of six deliveries by one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: To overspend is to spend more than one can afford, which is wasting money.

clue.text: It can go round either way

definitions.text: It can go round either way

blocks.clueFragment: It can go round either way
blocks.note: surface reading: something that spins clockwise or anticlockwise
setter's reading: the word itself reads the same forwards and backwards, as well as being a thing that spins

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a spinning part and also a palindrome, so it 'goes round' and reads the same in either direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor is the rotating part of a machine such as a helicopter or engine, and its letters mirror each other.

clue.text: Pulled off the road and tore away

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a road
ripped means tore, or tore away

explanation.surface: A driver pulled over to the roadside and then sped off again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulled off the road' reads as one phrase about driving, but the definition stops at 'Pulled off', as in pulling off clothes or paint.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip something is to pull or peel a covering off it, so stripped means pulled off.

clue.text: Without a pretext, respelt 'scene', perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters could be in another order, a possible version

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A word like scene might be rewritten with no excuse given.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Respelt' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the material; all twelve letters are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretence is a false excuse, so being pretenceless means having no pretext at all.

clue.text: Coach for all the business

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for a bus, a public passenger vehicle
second meaning: covering many items at once, as an all-in-one bill or edition does; the Latin original means 'for all'

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin root means 'for all', which is why the same word names a bus for everyone and a bill or edition gathering every item together.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnibus was a horse-drawn or motor bus, and an omnibus bill or volume bundles many separate items into one.

clue.text: One who forgives former cocaine drug addict

blocks.note: ex- means former, as in ex-wife
C is slang shorthand for cocaine
a user is someone who takes drugs

explanation.surface: A forgiving person turns out to be a former cocaine addict.
explanation.definitionFit: To excuse someone is to pardon them, so an excuser is a person who pardons.

clue.text: Titchy's not at long leg in the field

definitions.text: not at long leg in the field

blocks.note: first meaning: small, little

blocks.clueFragment: not at long leg in the field
blocks.note: second meaning: in cricket, the fielder close to the batsman rather than at long leg stands at the near version of that position

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, long leg is a fielding position far behind the batsman on the leg side; the close-in counterpart is called short leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Titchy is British slang for tiny, a synonym of little or small, and the cricket position near the bat is short leg.

clue.text: Smothering envoy, girl became disturbed

indicators.note: something disturbed is jumbled out of its order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman was upset when a diplomat hugged her too tightly.
explanation.definitionFit: To overlie is to lie on top of and suffocate, as of a baby, so overlying means smothering.

clue.text: Sustaining units sent all over the place

indicators.note: things scattered all over the place are in disorder, so these letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Supply units that keep troops going have been dispatched in every direction.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a rare word from the Latin for 'holding up'; the anagram and the crossings fix it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sustinent is a rare adjective meaning upholding or supporting, from Latin sustinere, to hold up.

clue.text: Established the exact moment Albert went first

blocks.note: inst. is the abbreviation for instant, the very moment
Al is short for Albert
led means went in front

explanation.surface: Someone pinned down the moment when Albert was ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went first' looks like an order instruction placing Albert at the front, but it supplies its own three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To install someone or something is to set it up in place, so installed means established.

clue.text: Exploits duties about the Queen

indicators.note: about means surrounding here, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: excises are taxes on goods, duties
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Someone takes advantage of the taxes levied around the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exploits' looks like a noun for daring deeds, but it is the verb: to exercise a right is to make use of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To exercise a power or right is to use it, so exercises works as a synonym of exploits, makes use of.

clue.text: The ICC step wrongfully on the doubting Thomas

indicators.note: something done wrongfully is done improperly, so the letters fall out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Cricket's governing body treads unfairly on someone who doubts it.
explanation.walkthrough: The ICC is the International Cricket Council; Thomas the apostle doubted the Resurrection until he saw proof.
explanation.definitionFit: A doubting Thomas is a person who refuses to believe without proof, a sceptic.

clue.text: Home Counties' doctor maybe more confident

blocks.note: the Home Counties surround London in the south-east of England
a doctor is one example of someone who cures

explanation.surface: A GP from the countryside round London might be more self-assured.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties around London, all in England's south-east, hence SE.
explanation.definitionFit: Secure can mean feeling safe and certain, so securer is more confident.

clue.text: InIreland, John locates Dutch car

indicators.note: to locate something is to give it a place, so one word is set inside the other

blocks.note: Sean is the Irish form of the name John
D is the abbreviation for Dutch

explanation.surface: An Irishman tracks down a car made in the Netherlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch car' reads as one thing, but Dutch only supplies a letter and car alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedan is a saloon car, the usual American and older British name for that body style.

clue.text: Colleague steals gold from his high school

indicators.note: whatever is stolen is taken away, so those letters leave the word

blocks.note: taken as written
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A fellow worker pockets gold from the school he once attended.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the A and the U of COLLEAGUE to leave COLLEGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Many British secondary schools are called colleges, such as Eton College, so college can stand for a high school.

clue.text: Choose the particle Ron left behind

indicators.note: whatever is left behind does not come along, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: an electron is a subatomic particle
taken as written

explanation.surface: Pick the speck that someone called Ron forgot to take.
explanation.definitionFit: To elect is to select by vote or decision, so it means choose.

clue.text: Pantomime produced by swine entwined with another animal

indicators.note: strands that are entwined are twisted together, so the letters of both words get mixed up

blocks.note: a swine is a contemptible man, a cad
a hare is a further animal after the swine

explanation.surface: A pantomime featuring a pig wrapped around some other creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swine' looks like the animal, but here it is an insult for a man; the true animal is the other one.
explanation.definitionFit: A charade is a mimed performance, and pantomime can mean acting by gesture alone, a silent show.

clue.text: Could be near a battlefield

indicators.note: could be says the letters may become something else, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something might lie close to the site of a battle.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a place of conflict or contest, a figurative battlefield, as in the political arena.

clue.text: Head of the top dog

blocks.note: first meaning: the person in charge of an organisation
second meaning: the boss, the most powerful person

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a dog's head; both halves actually describe someone in charge of a company.
explanation.definitionFit: A director runs a company or department, so is its head and its boss.

clue.text: Lord, for example, found in lounge

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to lounge is to lie about
e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A nobleman, say, discovered relaxing in the sitting room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lord, for example' reads as one phrase, but the comma splits it: Lord is the definition and 'for example' feeds the wordplay. 'Lounge' is the verb, not the room.
explanation.definitionFit: A liege is a feudal superior to whom allegiance is owed, a lord.

clue.text: Twenty-four points

blocks.note: surface reading: a score or tally, perhaps in a game
setter's reading: points on a British football pools coupon, where the best result type earns three points and eight selections are made

explanation.walkthrough: On the British football pools (Treble Chance), punters pick eight matches and a draw with goals scores 3 points, so eight of them make the maximum 24.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight matches drawn with goals, each worth three pools points, total exactly twenty-four, the jackpot line.
